analysis.one_liner: Loosens federal securities rules so young companies can go public and raise money with less disclosure.
analysis.headline: It became law on April 5, 2012, after the House passed it 390-23 and the Senate 73-26; Republicans supported it unanimously at every vote, most Democrats split, and President Obama signed it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new class of "emerging growth companies" — firms with under $1 billion in annual revenue — and exempts them for up to five years from several disclosure rules: they can go public with only two years of audited financials, skip the Sarbanes-Oxley internal-controls audit, and avoid a shareholder vote on executive pay and golden parachutes. It lets the investment banks that take a company public publish research reports about it, and lets companies quietly seek out big and wealthy investors before an offering. A separate set of titles lets companies advertise private offerings to accredited investors, creates a "crowdfunding" exemption so small investors can put money into startups through registered portals with per-investor limits, raises from 500 to 2,000 the number of shareholders a company can have before it must report to the SEC, and preempts some state securities oversight.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies going public or staying private longer, venture capital and private equity firms, investment banks that underwrite stock offerings, and a new crowdfunding platform industry. The stated aim is cheaper capital and more startups going public, which supporters argued would create jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Issuers, venture capital, underwriters, crowdfunding platforms

how_it_helps.text: Companies with under $1 billion in revenue can go public presenting only two years of audited financial statements and may delay complying with new accounting standards until larger companies must comply.
Emerging growth companies are exempt from the Sarbanes-Oxley requirement that an outside auditor attest to management's assessment of internal financial controls.
They are also exempt from the Dodd-Frank requirement for a separate shareholder vote on executive compensation, including golden parachute payments.

Broker-dealers participating in an offering may publish research reports about the company they are taking public, and the SEC is barred from adopting conflict-of-interest rules restricting analyst communications in these IPOs.
Companies may confidentially submit a draft registration statement to SEC staff for review before the public filing, and may sound out large institutional and accredited investors in advance.

The crowdfunding exemption lets ordinary people invest small amounts, capped by income and net worth, in startups through registered brokers or funding portals, with fraud-screening and disclosure requirements.

Companies may publicly advertise private securities offerings so long as every buyer is a verified accredited investor, and companies can grow to 2,000 shareholders before federal reporting is required.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary investors, who buy IPO shares with thinner financial statements, no independent audit opinion on internal controls, and research from the same banks selling the stock. Small crowdfunding investors take on startup risk the bill acknowledges up front. State securities regulators lose some authority to review offerings and police funding portals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retail investors and state securities regulators

drawbacks.text: Investors in a new public company may get only two years of audited financials and no auditor attestation on internal controls, meaning weaker assurance that the numbers and controls are sound.
Executives at companies under $1 billion in revenue no longer need a shareholder vote on their pay or golden parachutes, which had been a core Dodd-Frank investor right.

The bill authorizes the pre-IPO research reports that the SEC had restricted after analysts at underwriting banks promoted companies their own banks were selling, and it bars new conflict-of-interest rules for those IPOs.

Companies can now advertise private offerings to accredited investors — which changes how and to whom private investment funds can be marketed — while retail investors see none of those deals and lose nothing they had, but public markets gain fewer new listings.

Crowdfunding lets untested companies raise from small investors, with the statute itself requiring investors to affirm they understand they can lose their entire investment; fraud screening rests on the portals and SEC rulemaking.
Bank holding companies can stay outside SEC reporting until they have 2,000 shareholders of record, keeping bank ownership and financial information out of public view longer.
Funding platforms are shielded from most state securities laws, limiting a layer of local enforcement against fraud.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There are real gains here: cheaper IPOs, more small-company access to capital, and ordinary people getting legal access to startup investing they previously lacked. But the design puts most of the cost on the other side of the same trade — the information and audit checks that let ordinary investors price a stock are stripped for a decade's worth of companies with up to $1 billion in revenue, and the pay-vote and analyst-conflict protections lost were recent, deliberate safeguards. The honest verdict is a genuine capital-formation benefit purchased by a broad, permanent reduction in investor protection.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 390-23, the Senate amended it and passed it 73-26, the House agreed to the Senate version 380-41, and President Obama signed it on April 5, 2012.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee ordered the bill reported 54-1, and the full House passed it 390-23 with Republicans voting 232-0 in favor and Democrats voting 158-23.

House Democrats' floor amendments failed on voice votes, and a motion to require the company to disclose its political spending to the FEC failed 170-244, with 169 of 191 Democrats in favor and 232 of 241 Republicans opposed.

In the Senate, Majority Leader Reid's motion to send the bill to the Banking Committee with instructions to add an amendment failed when cloture was invoked 76-22, with Republicans voting 45-0 for and Democrats splitting 30-21.
The Senate passed its amended version 73-26, with Democrats splitting 26-25 and Republicans 46-0, and the House accepted the Senate amendment 380-41 on a suspension vote requiring two-thirds.
President Obama signed the bill on April 5, 2012, making it Public Law 112-106.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies going public, venture capital and private equity firms, investment banks that underwrite IPOs, and the new crowdfunding platform industry came out ahead. Ordinary investors got lighter disclosure standards on new public companies and no compensating enforcement strength; the disclosure mandates Democrats sought were stripped at every stage.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans voted for it unanimously at every stage — 232-0 in the House, 46-0 in the Senate — while Democrats split, 158-23 in the House, 26-25 in the Senate, and a Democratic president signed it into law.

industries.industry: Emerging growth companies under $1 billion in revenue
industries.note: The bill exempts them for up to five years from the internal-controls audit, most recent accounting standards, only-two-year financials on IPO, and the shareholder vote on executive pay. Their gain comes directly from giving investors less information and less say, though the opt-out provision lets a company voluntarily comply.

industries.industry: Venture capital and private equity firms
industries.note: They can now advertise private offerings to accredited investors and back companies that stay private longer before the 2,000-shareholder reporting trigger. This gives funds and their wealthy investors more room, while ordinary investors have no access to those deals and public markets get fewer new listings.

Banks taking a company public may again publish research reports about it, and the SEC is barred from applying conflict-of-interest rules to analyst communications in these IPOs. The arrangement pairs the analysts' imprimatur with the bank's own sale of the stock, and the information gap lands on retail investors.

The bill creates a new, SEC-registered intermediary industry between small investors and startups. It gives ordinary people legal access to startup investing for the first time, but with income-capped investments, required risk acknowledgments, and oversight that depends on SEC rulemaking and self-regulatory exams.

They can grow to 2,000 shareholders of record before having to register and report to the SEC, keeping ownership and financial details out of public view longer. Bank shareholders and depositors lose the transparency that registration provides.

Auditors lose the Sarbanes-Oxley internal-controls attestation engagement for emerging growth clients, reducing audit revenue. Their broader interest in issuer relationships generally ran with the bill's deregulatory direction.

Crowdfunding offerings and portals are shielded from most state registration review and fees, and the $50 million Regulation A exemption is also carved out from state law. States can still pursue fraud, but their gatekeeping role over local offerings is largely removed.
